graph_fundamentals.name: Graph Fundamentals and Representations
graph_fundamentals.definition: A Graph G = (V, E) is a non-linear data structure consisting of a finite set of vertices (or nodes) V and a set of edges E that connect pairs of vertices.
terminology: Vertex (Node): A fundamental data element in a graph.
Edge: An arc or link between two vertices (u, v).
Directed Graph (Digraph): Edges have direction (ordered pairs).
Undirected Graph: Edges are bidirectional (unordered pairs).
Weighted Graph: Edges carry numerical costs/weights.
Degree: In undirected graphs, number of connected edges. In directed graphs, split into In-degree and Out-degree.

representations.adjacency_matrix: A 2D array of size V x V where adj[i][j] = 1 if an edge exists between vertex i and j, else 0. Space: O(V^2). Efficient for dense graphs (edge lookup in O(1)).
representations.adjacency_list: An array of linked lists of size V where adjList[i] stores all adjacent vertices of i. Space: O(V + E). Efficient for sparse graphs.

graph_fundamentals.comparison_table:
| Parameter | Adjacency Matrix | Adjacency List |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Space Complexity** | O(V^2) | O(V + E) |
| **Edge Lookup (u, v)** | O(1) instantaneous | O(degree(u)) requires list search |
| **Add Vertex** | O(V^2) requires reallocating matrix | O(1) |
| **Best For** | Dense graphs (E ≈ V^2) | Sparse graphs (E << V^2) |

viva_questions.q: What is the space complexity of an Adjacency Matrix for a graph with V vertices?
viva_questions.a: O(V^2), regardless of the number of edges.

viva_questions.q: Why is an Adjacency List preferred for sparse graphs?
viva_questions.a: Sparse graphs have few edges (E << V^2). Adjacency list uses O(V + E) memory, whereas an adjacency matrix wastes massive memory storing zeroes (O(V^2)).

breadth_first_search.name: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
breadth_first_search.definition: Breadth-First Search (BFS) is a graph traversal algorithm that explores all vertices at the current depth/distance before moving on to vertices at the next depth level, using a FIFO Queue.
breadth_first_search.explanation: Starting at a source vertex, BFS marks it as visited and enqueues it. In each step, it dequeues a vertex, prints it, and visits/enqueues all its unvisited adjacent neighbors. It computes the shortest path in unweighted graphs.

breadth_first_search.time_complexity:
• Adjacency List: O(V + E)
• Adjacency Matrix: O(V^2)
breadth_first_search.space_complexity: O(V) auxiliary space for visited array and FIFO queue.
breadth_first_search.applications: Shortest path in unweighted graphs, GPS navigation, peer-to-peer torrent chunk discovery, web crawlers.

viva_questions.q: Which data structure is used to implement BFS?
Can BFS find the shortest path in a weighted graph?
viva_questions.a: No, standard BFS only guarantees the shortest path in UNWEIGHTED graphs. For non-negative weighted graphs, Dijkstra's algorithm is used.

depth_first_search.name: Depth-First Search (DFS)

• Adjacency List: O(V + E)
• Adjacency Matrix: O(V^2)
depth_first_search.applications: Cycle detection in directed/undirected graphs, Topological sorting for task build systems, solving mazes, bipartite graph checking.

viva_questions.q: What data structure does DFS use?
viva_questions.a: A LIFO Stack (either the system recursion call stack or an explicit stack data structure).

viva_questions.q: What is the difference between BFS and DFS?
viva_questions.a: BFS traverses level-by-level using a FIFO Queue and finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs. DFS dives deep down a single branch before backtracking using a LIFO Stack.
